prize_parts.citation: for the prediction of flat bands at the magic angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in it

statement.case_for: After the full first round my preferred configuration is unchanged: B033 as a single prize part, credited to MacDonald, Bistritzer and Jarillo-Herrero. The reason is the structure of the evidence, not the count of supporters. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model of 2011 made a quantitative, falsifiable statement that the Dirac velocity vanishes near a magic angle. The 2018 experiments found correlated insulators and superconductivity in devices at that angle, with the twist angle acting as a tunable control knob. Many groups have since reproduced the phase diagram in transport and STM, and extended it to other moire systems. The phenomenon is secure even though the pairing mechanism is not, and the committee has awarded prizes before for phenomena whose mechanism was open, provided the experimental facts were firmly established, as with the quantum Hall effects and cuprate superconductivity. The citation should be kept narrow: it honours the prediction and the discovery of the correlated phases, not an explanation of pairing and not the whole moire field. I did not find a competing configuration that is stronger on both science and attribution.
statement.case_against: The weaknesses are real and I will not play them down. First, the third seat: the committee has not yet verified the scope and dating of Andrei's pre-2018 STM and transport work. Second, the first authors of the 2018 papers (Cao in particular) and the Dean and Kim hBN device work are left out by the three-person limit. Third, sample-to-sample twist-angle disorder and strain mean the experimental phase diagram is device dependent, and as a DFT person I know that the continuum model is an idealisation: lattice relaxation shifts the magic angle and the bandwidth quantitatively, so we do not yet have a quantitative microscopic theory of the correlated phases. Fourth, the field is roughly seven years old as an experimental programme, so a reasonable colleague could say we should wait. I weigh these as caveats on a secure phenomenon, but they are why I keep B026 and B009 as serious fallbacks.

responses.point: Pearce asks me, as the condensed-matter specialist, whether Andrei's STM results were close enough to the 2011 prediction to count as priority, and says he would reconsider the third name if I judge that they were.
responses.response: I have thought about this carefully and my answer is that they were not close enough to displace Bistritzer. As I recall, and I flag that this is from memory and not checked against the papers, Andrei's group reported STM evidence of Van Hove singularities and strong localisation in twisted graphene layers around 2010. That showed that the twist can reconstruct the low-energy electronic structure, which is valuable and was ahead of the field. But it did not locate the magic angle, it did not claim flat bands as a quantitative prediction, and it did not show the correlated insulating or superconducting states that define the discovery claimed in the citation. The Bistritzer-MacDonald result is the first quantitative statement of why a specific angle is special, and the experiment tested exactly that. So on priority for this citation I place Andrei as a strong supporting contributor to the field, not as a co-discoverer of the cited result. I am treating this as a judgement that a prize committee has to make, and I would want the committee's expert report to check the dates before the vote.

responses.point: Mehlig insists that the logic of the citation is one clean mechanism, prediction followed by discovery, and prefers to admit that the attribution is imperfect rather than distort the citation by splitting the authors of the prediction paper.
responses.response: I agree, and this is the point that settled my own view in round 1. I would add a consequence for wording. If the citation is pinned to the prediction and to the correlated and superconducting states, then it is internally consistent that the third name is the second author of the prediction paper, and that leaving out Andrei, Cao, Dean and Kim is a limit of the statutes and not a verdict on their work. I share your concern about the pairing mechanism, but I do not think it should block the prize: the observation of superconductivity at the predicted flat-band angle is a fact that stands independently of the theory of pairing, which is why I would phrase the citation to avoid any claim about mechanism.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first because the concept is simple, the performance is verified between independent laboratories, and the two-name credit is the only one that fits the three-laureate limit without a painful split, while she admits the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I take this seriously, since it is the strongest competing case on the table and you applied exactly the criterion I use myself, namely independent confirmation by cross-checks. My difference is about what the prize should reward this year. The clocks are an extraordinary advance in an established measurement, and the overlap with 2005 and 2012 is something you yourself concede. Magic-angle graphene opens a new regime of correlated quantum matter. On the common standard the chair asked for, I would say that both have independent reproduction; B033 has sample dependence that clocks do not, and I count that against B033 modestly. I do not think the pending redefinition of the second should decide anything. If the committee finds B033's credit cannot be settled, B026 is my first fallback, ahead of B009.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that recognising the platform before the pairing mechanism is understood might look premature in hindsight, and agrees the third seat is the weakest part of the configuration.
responses.response: I think the hindsight risk is the right worry, and I would answer it by what has been independently shown, not by what is understood. Prizes in condensed matter have gone to established experimental phenomena with an open mechanism, and the evidence here is multi-group and multi-platform. I would change my view if sample dependence turned out to hide the superconductivity as an artefact, but the reproductions and the spread to twisted multilayers and transition-metal dichalcogenide moire systems make that unlikely.

uncertainties: My dating of Andrei's pre-2018 STM and transport results is from memory and should be verified before the final vote, since it is the one fact that could change the third name.
Whether the first authors of the 2018 papers and the hBN device pioneers (Dean, Kim) can be defended as outside the three seats; I think so under the statutes, but the committee should say it openly.
How much the unresolved pairing mechanism and relaxation effects in the continuum model should count against the maturity of B033.
For B009, whether Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is defensible without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang; I regard it only as a fallback.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict requiring recusal. I have no personal or institutional tie to MacDonald, Bistritzer, Jarillo-Herrero or Andrei. My DFT and atomistic spin-dynamics work is methodologically adjacent to moire materials, but not a collaboration or funding link. After round 1 I have no new disclosure to add.
